snip.t: Understanding that fibroblast activation, collagen over‑production and endothelial dysfunction are central helps link clinical signs to organ pathology.

Bronchial wall components – collagen, elastin, smooth‑muscle, submucosal glands: Inflammatory proteases (neutrophil elastase, matrix metalloproteinases) degrade elastin and collagen, thinning the wall and permitting outward expansion under airway pressure.
Expansion by oedema, cellular infiltrates or collagen replaces normal elastic recoil, producing a restrictive ventilatory pattern (reduced TLC, FVC).
Myofibroblast differentiation → excess collagen I/III, fibronectin, elastin deposition
Platelet adhesion: platelets stick to exposed collagen through von Willebrand factor (GPIb).

qs.q: A patient is evaluated for chronic liver disease. Histological examination of a liver biopsy shows fibrosis extending between portal triads and central veins. What are the primary collagen-secreting cells?
qs.e: Hepatic stellate cells store vitamin A and transform into myofibroblasts to secrete scar collagen.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Anatomy Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 50-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C develops progressive liver failure. Biopsy reveals nodules of regenerating hepatocytes separated by fibrous septa. Which hepatic cell type is primarily responsible for laying down the collagen scar tissue in this cirrhosis?
o: Hepatic stellate cells located in the space of Disse.
Kupffer cells anchored along the sinusoidal endothelial lining.
Portal vein endothelial cells undergoing mesenchymal transition.
Cholangiocytes proliferating around damaged interlobular ducts.
Fibroblasts migrating inward from the Glisson capsule.
qs.e: During chronic liver injury, hepatic stellate cells activate into myofibroblasts and secrete excessive extracellular matrix collagen.
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A plastic surgeon is planning an elective facial excision and wants to place the incision parallel to the natural orientation of collagen fibers in the dermis to minimize scarring. What are these guiding lines called?
qs.e: Langer's cleavage lines correspond to the natural orientation of collagen fibers in the dermis, and incisions made parallel to them heal with narrower scars. Incisions crossing these lines tend to gape and form hypertrophic scars.
qs.s: Basic Surgical Skills: Scrubbing, Sutures, Knots, Incisions,: MCQs

qs.q: During the fibroplasia and matrix deposition phase of healing, fibroblasts migrate into the wound and begin laying down collagen starting around which postoperative day?
qs.e: Fibroblasts deposit collagen and proteoglycans starting from about day 3 to 4, forming the physical basis of wound strength. Platelets and haemostasis occur earlier on day 0 to 3.
qs.s: Wound Healing: Phases, Types of Healing and Factors That Delay It: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with severe scurvy secondary to malnutrition experiences delayed wound healing because her fibroblasts fail to synthesize adequate collagen. Which specific biochemical step in collagen synthesis directly requires vitamin C?
o: Cleavage of type III into type I collagen
Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues
Cross-linking of collagen fibrils by MMPs
Aggregation of platelets into a fibrin plug
qs.e: Vitamin C, oxygen, iron, and zinc are required for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine during collagen synthesis. Collagenases and matrix metalloproteinases handle the subsequent remodelling and cross-linking.
qs.s: Wound Healing: Phases, Types of Healing and Factors That Delay It: MCQs

qs.q: During the remodelling phase of cutaneous wound healing which extends from 3 weeks up to 2 years, which enzyme family is primarily responsible for the continuous breakdown, restructuring, and cross-linking of collagen fibers?
qs.e: Collagenases and matrix metalloproteinases continually remodel and cross-link collagen during the maturation phase. Serine proteases are more active in the initial coagulation cascade rather than long-term scar remodeling.
qs.s: Wound Healing: Phases, Types of Healing and Factors That Delay It: MCQs

qs.q: An endoscopic evaluation of a patient with chronic watery diarrhoea and normal mucosal appearance reveals no gross lesions. However, biopsies demonstrate a dense subepithelial collagen layer beneath the surface epithelium. Which condition does this describe?
qs.e: Collagenous colitis is a type of microscopic colitis defined by a dense subepithelial collagen layer seen on biopsy despite normal endoscopic findings. Lymphocytic colitis features an increased number of intraepithelial lymphocytes instead.

qs.q: Which component of an atherosclerotic plaque directly overlies the necrotic core and consists primarily of smooth muscle cells and dense collagen?
qs.e: The fibrous cap overlies the lipid-rich necrotic core and provides structural stability, consisting of smooth muscle cells and dense collagen. A vulnerable plaque has a thin cap, making it prone to rupture.

es.q: Describe the three characteristic histological features of cirrhosis. Additionally, identify the key cell responsible for the pathogenesis of liver fibrosis and list two substances that stimulate this cell to produce collagen.
es.m: The three characteristic histological features of cirrhosis are: 1. Bridging fibrous septa (composed of collagen types I & III). 2. Disruption of the entire liver architecture. 3. Parenchymal regenerative nodules. The key cell responsible for the pathogenesis of liver fibrosis is the **Ito cell (hepatic stellate cell)**. It is stimulated by substances such as TGF-β, TNF, and IL-1 to produce collagen.
es.s: Liver Histology, Physiology and Pathology — Practice Questions

es.q: A liver biopsy report from a patient with a history of chronic alcohol abuse describes 'ballooning degeneration, Mallory bodies, and neutrophilic infiltration'. 1. Name the specific stage of alcoholic liver disease indicated by these histological features. 2. Describe the histological characteristic
es.m: 1. These histological features are characteristic of **Alcoholic Hepatitis**. 2. The earliest, reversible stage of alcoholic liver disease is **Hepatic Steatosis**, characterized by the accumulation of fat (triglycerides) within hepatocytes, making the liver appear soft, yellow, and greasy. 3. The key cell type responsible for collagen production in the development of fibrosis is the **Ito cell (hepatic stellate cell)**.
es.s: Liver Histology, Physiology and Pathology — Practice Questions

es.q: A liver biopsy from a chronic alcoholic patient reveals eosinophilic cytokeratin inclusions within hepatocytes, along with widespread collagen deposition forming regenerative nodules and bridging fibrous septa. Identify the specific histological findings described and explain what they indicate in t
es.m: Eosinophilic cytokeratin inclusions: These are characteristic **Mallory bodies**, a histological hallmark of alcoholic hepatitis. Collagen deposition, regenerative nodules, and bridging fibrous septa: These are the definitive histological features of **Cirrhosis**. Indication of Progression: The presence of Mallory bodies suggests ongoing alcoholic hepatitis. The concurrent finding of regenerative nodules and bridging fibrous septa confirms that the disease has progressed to end-stage liver disease, specifically alcoholic cirrhosis, characterized by irreversible disruption of liver architecture.
es.s: Liver Histology, Physiology and Pathology — Practice Questions

es.q: A liver biopsy is performed on a patient with suspected chronic liver disease. The pathologist observes the following distinct histological findings: 1. Acidophilic apoptotic hepatocytes 2. Eosinophilic cytokeratin inclusions within hepatocytes 3. Collagen deposition forming regenerative nodules and
es.m: 1. **Councilman bodies**: These are acidophilic apoptotic hepatocytes, typically associated with acute viral hepatitis. 2. **Mallory bodies**: These are eosinophilic cytokeratin inclusions found within hepatocytes, classically associated with alcoholic hepatitis, but also seen in Wilson's disease and NASH (Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis). 3. **Cirrhosis**: This describes a pattern of end-stage liver disease characterized by diffuse fibrosis (collagen types I & III forming bridging septa) and the formation of parenchymal regenerative nodules, leading to disrupted liver architecture. It can be micronodular (e.g., alcoholic) or macronodular (e.g., viral hepatitis).
es.s: Liver Histology, Physiology and Pathology — Practice Questions — Essay Questions

ai.summary: Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body, serving as the primary structural component of the extracellular matrix (ECM) in connective tissues such as skin, bone, cartilage, and blood vessels.

sections.p: Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body, serving as the primary structural component of the extracellular matrix (ECM) in connective tissues such as skin, bone, cartilage, and blood vessels.

b: Amino Acid Composition: Characterized by a repeating sequence of (Gly-X-Y), where X is often proline and Y is hydroxyproline or hydroxylysine.
Triple Helix: Three polypeptide alpha-chains wind around each other to form a stable rope-like structure.
Post-translational Modification:
Hydroxylation: Requires Vitamin C (Ascorbate) and iron. Deficiency leads to scurvy.
Glycosylation: Addition of glucose/galactose to hydroxylysine residues.
Cross-linking: Lysyl oxidase (copper-dependent) creates covalent bonds between collagen fibrils to provide tensile strength.
Type I: Bone, skin, tendons, and late wound healing (scar). Most common.
Type II: Cartilage and vitreous body.
Type III (Reticulin): Blood vessels, fetal skin, and early wound healing.
Type IV: Basement membrane (lamina densa).
Osteogenesis Imperfecta: Genetic defect (usually Type I) leading to brittle bones, blue sclerae, and hearing loss.
Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome: Group of disorders affecting collagen synthesis (e.g., Type III or V), resulting in hypermobile joints and hyperextensible skin.
Alport Syndrome: Defect in Type IV collagen affecting the basement membrane of the kidney (glomerulonephritis), ears, and eyes.
Elastin: Unlike collagen, elastin lacks a triple helix, contains desmosine cross-links, and provides recoil rather than tensile strength.
Reticulin: Once thought distinct, these are actually Type III collagen fibers that form delicate branched networks in lymphoid organs.
Normal collagen levels in Scurvy: The total amount of collagen may appear normal initially, but the lack of hydroxylation makes the fibers functionally defective.
Biopsy limitations: A skin biopsy might show normal collagen architecture in early stages of certain systemic connective tissue diseases.

faq.q: What is the basic structural unit of collagen?
faq.a: The tropocollagen molecule, consisting of a triple helix of three polypeptide alpha chains stabilized by hydrogen bonding.

faq.q: Why is Vitamin C essential for collagen synthesis?
faq.a: It acts as a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase enzymes, which hydroxylate amino acids to allow stable cross-linking.

faq.q: Which amino acid is most abundant in collagen?
faq.a: Glycine occurs at every third position (Gly-X-Y) because its small size allows it to fit in the tight central core of the helix.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Collect a focused history and perform a systematic examination to detect collagen‑related disorders, noting skin, joint, and wound features, and to rule out mimics.
b: Ask about easy bruising, joint hypermobility, frequent fractures, hearing loss, blue sclerae, skin fragility, and family history of brittle bones or skin problems.
Check for chronic wounds that heal slowly or with excessive scarring.
Inquire about gastrointestinal bleeding or protein‑losing enteropathy.
Ask about recurrent hernias or abdominal wall laxity.
Look for visual disturbances or hearing loss.
Ask about pregnancy history and any drug or herbal use that could affect collagen.
Check for signs of systemic disease such as renal or liver dysfunction.
Record any history of atherosclerotic disease or vascular events.

t.b: Look for thin, translucent skin, stretch marks, and bruising; a positive finding suggests collagen fragility.
Test for hypermobility using the Beighton score; >4 indicates connective tissue disorder.
Note delayed healing or hypertrophic/keloid scars; suggests abnormal collagen deposition.
Blue or gray sclerae point to osteogenesis imperfecta.
Tympanometry or audiometry for sensorineural loss; common in osteogenesis imperfecta.
Palpate for organomegaly or ascites; may indicate systemic collagen disease.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use laboratory and imaging tests to quantify collagen synthesis, detect deficiencies, and assess organ involvement.

t.b: <11.4 µmol/L (<0.2 mg/dL) confirms scurvy; normal range 11.4–25 µmol/L.
<70 µg/dL indicates lysyl oxidase deficiency; normal 70–140 µg/dL.
Elevated levels (>10 nmol/mmol creatinine) suggest increased bone collagen degradation, seen in osteogenesis imperfecta.

t.a: Serum procollagen type I N‑terminal propeptide (PINP)
t.b: Normal adult range 30–100 µg/L; values >100 µg/L indicate active type I collagen synthesis.

t.a: Serum procollagen type I C‑terminal propeptide (PICP)
t.b: Normal adult range 100–300 µg/L; values above the upper limit suggest active fibrosis.
>100 µg/L indicates significant hepatic fibrosis; lower values may still reflect fibrosis.
Positive indicates functional platelet‑collagen interaction; negative may suggest platelet dysfunction.
Shows collagen density and arrangement; thickened subepithelial band indicates collagenous colitis.
Defects suggest Alport syndrome.
Assess for ventricular wall thickness; concentric hypertrophy indicates chronic pressure overload.

sections.p: Apply established criteria to classify collagen disorders and gauge disease burden.
b: Osteogenesis imperfecta: Clinical triad of fractures, blue sclerae, and hearing loss; confirmed by COL1A1/A2 mutations.
Ehlers‑Danlos spectrum: Hypermobile type—Beighton score >4; classical type—skin hyperextensibility, atrophic scarring; vascular type—COL3A1 mutation.
Collagenous colitis: Subepithelial collagen band >10 µm on biopsy; symptom severity graded by stool frequency and weight loss.
Alport syndrome: Hematuria, sensorineural deafness, ocular changes; confirmed by type IV collagen mutation.

t.b: >4 indicates joint hypermobility; used for Ehlers‑Danlos diagnosis.
Supports osteogenesis imperfecta.
Denotes advanced hepatic fibrosis.
Diagnostic of collagenous colitis.

sections.p: Differentiate collagen disorders from other diseases with similar features.

t.b: Tall stature, arachnodactyly, aortic root dilation; differentiate by FBN1 mutation and absence of skin fragility.
Malar rash, photosensitivity; differentiate by ANA positivity and systemic features.
Skin thickening, Raynaud's phenomenon; differentiate by CREST features and anti‑Scl‑70 antibodies.
Gottron papules, heliotrope rash; differentiate by muscle weakness and elevated CK.
Arterial rupture, easy bruising; differentiate by COL3A1 mutation and absence of joint hypermobility.

sections.p: Approach to disorders of collagen synthesis or excess, focusing on scurvy, Ehlers‑Danlos, osteogenesis imperfecta and fibrotic liver disease.
b: 1. Confirm diagnosis with targeted history, exam and appropriate investigations before treatment.
2. Replace deficient cofactors (vitamin C, copper, iron) as first‑line therapy for synthesis defects.

3. Use disease‑specific agents: bisphosphonates for osteogenesis imperfecta, physiotherapy and splinting for Ehlers‑Danlos, antifibrotic measures (e.g., lifestyle, antiviral therapy) for liver fibrosis.
4. Monitor biochemical markers (PICP, PINP, hyaluronic acid) and clinical response; repeat at 3‑month intervals.
5. Escalate to specialist referral when fractures are recurrent, wound healing fails, or fibrosis progresses despite basic measures.

t.b: Ask about bruising, joint hypermobility, recurrent fractures, dietary intake of citrus, alcohol use, and family history of connective‑tissue disorders.
Inspect skin for hyperextensible joints, scar type, bruises; palpate tendon laxity (Beighton score); assess bone tenderness; look for hepatomegaly or ascites in fibrosis.
Serum vitamin C, copper, iron; urinary pyridinoline; genetic testing for COL1A1/2, COL3A1; liver elastography; biopsy when diagnosis uncertain.
Any child with >1 fracture without trauma, progressive liver stiffness, or severe malnutrition requiring multidisciplinary care.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key adverse effects of agents used in collagen‑related conditions and how to manage them.
b: Bisphosphonates may cause acute phase reaction (fever, myalgia); give antipyretics and hydrate.
High‑dose vitamin C can precipitate oxalate kidney stones; ensure adequate hydration and monitor renal function.
Copper supplementation can cause gastrointestinal upset; give with meals and watch for copper‑induced liver enzyme rise.
Antifibrotic agents (e.g., angiotensin‑II blockers) may lower blood pressure; monitor orthostatic symptoms.
Avoid NSAIDs in severe liver fibrosis as they increase bleeding risk.

t.b: Vitamin C enhances iron absorption – separate iron tablets from calcium to avoid competition.
Check serum creatinine after bisphosphonate infusion; repeat urinary calcium if high‑dose vitamin C is used.

sections.p: Potential sequelae of untreated collagen disorders and criteria for urgent action.
b: Recurrent fractures → risk of deformity; arrange orthopedic review if >2 fractures in 6 weeks.
Progressive hepatic fibrosis → development of portal hypertension; refer for endoscopy when platelet count <150 ×10⁹/L or splenomegaly appears.
Severe scurvy → hemorrhagic gums, anemia; admit for intravenous vitamin C if oral intake impossible.
Joint dislocations in Ehlers‑Danlos → neurovascular compromise; urgent imaging and surgical consult if neuro signs present.
Keloid overgrowth causing functional limitation → consider intralesional steroids after failure of pressure therapy.

t.b: PICP or PINP rising above the laboratory‑specific upper limit on two consecutive tests warrants escalation.
New onset ascites, encephalopathy, or variceal bleeding in liver disease demands immediate specialist input.

sections.p: Conditions that modify presentation, test interpretation or treatment of collagen abnormalities.
b: HIV infection can lower vitamin C levels and increase oxidative stress, worsening scurvy‑like features.
Active tuberculosis may cause chronic inflammation that raises serum collagen markers independent of fibrosis.
Malnutrition reduces availability of proline, lysine and vitamin C; supplement with balanced nutrition before relying on lab values.
Pregnancy increases plasma volume, diluting serum collagen peptides; adjust reference ranges accordingly.
Diabetes impairs wound healing and may mask scar quality; monitor glycaemic control closely.
Alcohol directly damages hepatocytes and stimulates stellate cell activation, accelerating fibrosis.
Renal failure reduces clearance of collagen turnover markers, leading to falsely high levels.
Extreme ages: infants have higher collagen turnover; elderly have reduced synthesis, affecting both diagnosis and therapy.

t.b: Rely on clinical signs (gingival bleeding, perifollicular hemorrhage) and dietary history.
Use serum hyaluronic acid and platelet count as surrogate fibrosis indicators.

sections.p: Tailored considerations for children, pregnant women, the elderly and low‑resource environments.
b: Children with suspected osteogenesis imperfecta: prioritize gentle handling, physiotherapy, and oral bisphosphonates; avoid high‑impact sports.
Pregnant women: give oral vitamin C (≥85 mg/day) and copper; avoid teratogenic antifibrotics; monitor fetal growth if liver fibrosis present.
Elderly: start with low‑dose vitamin C to avoid renal stones; assess renal function before bisphosphonates; watch for polypharmacy interactions.
People with HIV: ensure antiretroviral regimen does not include protease inhibitors that impair fibroblast function; supplement vitamin C and copper.

Low‑resource settings: use dietary sources (citrus, leafy greens) for vitamin C, inexpensive copper‑rich foods (nuts, legumes); employ bedside liver stiffness assessment with portable FibroScan if available, otherwise use platelet‑to‑splenic‑size ratio.

t.b: List three bedside signs of scurvy and explain why they occur.

facts: Normal serum PICP varies 100‑300 µg/L (age‑dependent); values above reference suggest active type I collagen synthesis.
Normal serum PINP ranges 30‑100 µg/L (age‑dependent); elevated levels indicate increased collagen turnover.
Serum hyaluronic acid >100 µg/L is highly suggestive of advanced hepatic fibrosis or cirrhosis.
Serum vitamin C <0.2 mg/dL (or <11.4 µmol/L) is diagnostic of scurvy; clinical signs may appear before this level.
Serum copper <70 µg/dL indicates potential lysyl‑oxidase deficiency; treat with copper sulphate if low.
Urinary pyridinoline cross‑links >10 nmol/mmol creatinine suggests increased bone collagen degradation in osteogenesis imperfecta.
Platelet GpIb‑VWF interaction requires the platelet surface receptor GpIbα; this is the primary bridge for adhesion to exposed subendothelial collagen.
Type I collagen fibrils are cross‑linked by lysyl oxidase, a copper‑dependent enzyme; deficiency leads to fragile connective tissue.

vivas.q: What is the key intracellular step in collagen synthesis that requires vitamin C?
vivas.a: Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylation of the Gly‑X‑Y repeat; vitamin C is a cofactor for the hydroxylases.

vivas.q: Which platelet receptor binds von Willebrand factor on exposed subendothelial collagen?
vivas.a: GpIbα; this interaction initiates platelet adhesion in primary haemostasis.

vivas.q: Describe the histological appearance of a dense subepithelial collagen layer in chronic watery diarrhoea.
vivas.a: A thickened subepithelial collagen band beneath normal epithelium; typical of collagenous colitis.

vivas.q: Which component of an atherosclerotic plaque directly overlies the necrotic core and is rich in smooth muscle cells and dense collagen?
vivas.a: The fibrous cap; it is composed mainly of smooth muscle cells and collagen.

vivas.q: What is the biochemical modification of type II collagen antigens in rheumatoid arthritis?
vivas.a: Autoantibodies target citrullinated peptides; citrullination is a post‑translational modification of arginine residues.

vivas.q: Why is a patient with an excessive scar confined within wound boundaries considered a hypertrophic scar?
vivas.a: Hypertrophic scars have excess collagen (type I and III) but do not extend beyond the original wound edges.

vivas.q: What type of necrosis occurs in brain tissue after arterial occlusion due to lack of collagen framework?
vivas.a: Liquefactive necrosis; the high lipid content and absence of structural collagen promote enzymatic digestion.

vivas.q: Which hepatic cell type produces collagen types I and III during fibrosis?
vivas.a: Hepatic stellate cells (Ito cells); they activate and secrete collagen during liver injury.

vivas.q: Name the three characteristic histological features of cirrhosis.
vivas.a: Fibrous septa, regenerative nodules, and nodular liver architecture; these reflect chronic fibrosis and regeneration.

vivas.q: What is the key cell responsible for liver fibrosis and two substances that stimulate it?
vivas.a: Hepatic stellate cells; activated by transforming growth factor‑β (TGF‑β) and platelet‑derived growth factor (PDGF).

vivas.q: What stage of alcoholic liver disease is indicated by ballooning degeneration, Mallory bodies, and neutrophilic infiltration?
vivas.a: Alcoholic hepatitis; this is an acute inflammatory stage of chronic alcohol abuse.

vivas.q: In a chronic alcoholic liver biopsy with eosinophilic cytokeratin inclusions and bridging fibrosis, what is the diagnosis?
vivas.a: Alcoholic cirrhosis; the inclusions are Mallory–Denk bodies and bridging fibrosis indicates advanced scarring.

vivas.q: What bedside sign is used to differentiate a hypertrophic scar from a keloid?
vivas.a: Hypertrophic scars are confined to wound edges; keloids extend beyond the original scar border.

vivas.q: Why is iron supplementation avoided in patients with active collagen synthesis disorders?
vivas.a: Excess iron can generate oxidative stress; however, iron is a cofactor for hydroxylases, so deficiency—not excess—impairs collagen.

vivas.q: How would you manage a patient with scurvy presenting with bleeding gums and poor wound healing?
vivas.a: Give oral vitamin C 500–1000 mg/day; monitor clinical improvement and serum vitamin C levels.

mcqs.q: A 35‑year‑old woman with recurrent easy bruising and translucent skin has a skin biopsy showing abundant type III collagen. Which mutation is most likely?
mcqs.e: COL3A1 mutation causes vascular Ehlers‑Danlos syndrome.

mcqs.q: Which laboratory value best indicates active hepatic fibrosis?
mcqs.e: Hyaluronic acid >100 µg/L is highly suggestive of advanced fibrosis.

mcqs.q: A patient with chronic watery diarrhoea has a normal mucosal appearance but a dense subepithelial collagen band. What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.e: Collagenous colitis shows a thickened subepithelial collagen layer.

mcqs.q: Which enzyme cross‑links collagen fibrils and requires copper?
mcqs.e: Lysyl oxidase is copper‑dependent and forms covalent cross‑links.

mcqs.q: A 28‑year‑old man with blue sclerae and frequent fractures is found to have a mutation in COL1A1. Which condition does he have?
Which of the following is NOT a typical feature of a hypertrophic scar?
o: Firm, raised, confined to wound edges
mcqs.e: Hypertrophic scars do not spread beyond the original wound edges.

cases.v: A 22‑year‑old woman presents with painless, firm, raised lesions on her forearms that have not extended beyond the original wound edges. She reports frequent bruising and easy tearing of skin. Examination shows translucent skin and mild joint hypermobility.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a: Hypertrophic scar formation secondary to a connective tissue disorder, likely Ehlers‑Danlos syndrome type III.

qs.q: Which laboratory test would confirm the diagnosis?
qs.a: Serum PICP and PINP levels to assess collagen synthesis; genetic testing for COL3A1 mutations.

qs.q: What is the first step in management?
qs.a: Counsel on skin protection, advise avoidance of trauma, and consider physiotherapy for joint stability.

cases.v: A 45‑year‑old man with a history of chronic alcohol abuse presents with jaundice, ascites, and asterixis. Liver biopsy shows ballooning degeneration, Mallory bodies, and bridging fibrosis. He has a serum hyaluronic acid level of 120 µg/L.

qs.q: What stage of alcoholic liver disease does he have?
qs.a: Alcoholic cirrhosis; the biopsy shows bridging fibrosis and nodular regeneration.

qs.q: Which serum marker indicates advanced fibrosis?
What is the next best management step?
qs.a: Initiate portal hypertension management with beta‑blockers and consider referral for liver transplantation evaluation.

mistakes: Confusing hypertrophic scars with keloids as both being only type III collagen.
Using 150 µg/L as a universal cut‑off for active fibrosis without lab reference ranges.
Assuming iron excess impairs collagen synthesis; deficiency is the problem.
Mislabeling the platelet receptor for VWF as GpIbβ instead of GpIbα.
Overlooking that urinary pyridinoline cross‑links are elevated in osteogenesis imperfecta but not a diagnostic cut‑off.
Failing to differentiate type I and III collagen in scar pathology.
Ignoring that serum vitamin C <0.2 mg/dL is diagnostic of scurvy, not just clinical signs.
Misinterpreting a dense subepithelial collagen band as a normal finding rather than collagenous colitis.
